description: Hi, I'm Marwa, an engineering student at ENSA passionate about Earth observation, data, and innovation for a better planet. I'm building a friendly, motivated team to create a creative, data-driven solution with NASA open data. Looking for a developer, a data/AI person, a designer, and a great presenter. Beginners welcome! 🚀
summary: The Changing Rainfall is a Trend Detective project that asks whether Earth’s rainfall is really changing or just swinging naturally. We looked at precipitation from 2006 to 2026, moving from the whole planet down to one country, Morocco. We used NASA GPM IMERG satellite data at about 10 km resolution, NASA MERRA-2 for the global view, and CRU records and dam data as cross-checks. We built an interactive website and a short presentation that show Morocco’s sharp north-south gradient, with the north receiving about 5x more rain than the south. A Theil-Sen slope and Mann-Kendall test show a drying trend of about -5.7 mm per year. The last decade got 22% less rain than the one before. We link this to falling dam levels, a weaker wheat harvest and water cuts. We state the limits plainly: the record is short, and a pattern is not proof of a cause. Rain is changing, and water security depends on how we respond.
details:
What it does

The Changing Rainfall is an interactive story that asks one question: is Earth’s rain really changing, or are we just seeing natural swings? It starts with the whole planet and narrows to Morocco, a country between the Atlantic and the Sahara. It uses NASA satellite data to show where rain falls, how it has changed since 2006, and what that means for people.

How it works

We processed NASA GPM IMERG V07 rainfall data at 0.1° resolution (about 10 km). That gave 4,194 grid cells over Morocco, which we mapped and averaged. The map shows a clear gradient: 38.3 mm/month in the north versus 7.3 mm/month in the south. We also built a 3D rainfall terrain, where column height and colour show rainfall. For the global view we used NASA MERRA-2 through Giovanni. To test whether a trend is real, we used a Theil-Sen slope and a Mann-Kendall test on yearly rainfall. The result is -5.7 mm per year (p = 0.003). The last decade also received 22% less rain than the decade before.

Benefits and intended impact

The project turns complex climate data into a clear story anyone can follow. It links rainfall to dam levels, wheat harvests, and drinking water cuts, so people can see how changes in rain affect daily life. We hope it helps students, communities, and decision-makers understand water risk and plan for both drought and floods.

Tools and data

  • NASA GPM IMERG V07 (Final Run), NASA MERRA-2, and NASA GES DISC / Giovanni
  • CRU TS for the yearly series
  • Ministry of Equipment and Water reservoir data, via Morocco World News and Le360
  • HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the website and presentation, with a canvas-based 3D terrain
  • Netlify for hosting

What makes it creative

We framed the project as a “Trend Detective” case. Instead of just showing charts, we ask whether a pattern is a trend or just noise. The scale zoom from the planet to one country, the 3D terrain, and the chain from rainfall to nature to cities to people make the data feel tangible.

Factors we considered

We tried to be honest about the evidence:

  • Twenty years is a short record.
  • The TRMM-to-GPM join in 2014 can affect trends.
  • Satellite estimates are weaker over mountains and deserts.
  • We never mix data versions or units, and missing data stays missing.
  • We treat a link as a pattern, not proof of a cause.
  • The 2025-26 wet winter is not yet in the yearly series.
